name: The Human Dead
summary: No claws, no scales, nothing in the blood. What humans brought to Nangijala instead was a habit of telling each other things, and it turned out to be the only thing that mattered.
body: Of everything that falls out of the sky into Nangijala, the human dead are neither the oldest nor the strongest nor the strangest, and they know it. A human arrives with no claws, no scales, nothing in the blood, and nothing to trade on but nerve and a quick pair of hands.
What they do have is a habit, and the habit turns out to be the most important fact about this world.

Humans talk. Not usefully, most of the time — they talk about the weather, and about people who are not present, and about what happened to them once in a place that no longer exists. They do it at the ends of days. They do it around fires, without being asked, as though something in them cannot sit in front of a light with another person and stay quiet.

In any other country that would be a pleasant nothing. Here it is maintenance. Every one of those idle evenings is a thing being held in shape, and the reason so much of Nangijala is still standing is that a species which cannot stop chattering fell into a world that is built out of being talked about. The fire-keepers did not invent the practice. They only noticed what everybody was already doing and wrote a rota for it.

It has made humans, on the whole, the ones who go and meet the stars. Not out of any particular virtue — they are as petty here as anywhere and the arguments in this world are almost all theirs — but because a human who sees a light come down over the next field is constitutionally incapable of not walking over to see who it was.

They are also the ones who fight, which follows from the same thing rather than from any talent for it. A human will go a long way out of their way for somebody they have sat with. Give them a reason and a blade and they will walk into the black rock after a thing that has nothing left in it, and come back with a warm stone in their pocket and a story about it, and tell the story that night, and hold up a corner of the world for another year without ever once thinking of it that way.

They fall young and they fall old and they fall in every state of readiness. Most arrive with nothing but what they stand in. Nearly all of them, given a season and somebody to listen, get their name back.
